description: ICL10's plan written for the condition, the eye_injury flow's plan, and plans for the other six example rows built only from their DEMO-CONDITIONS.md lines.

sources.title: British Heart Foundation, Checking your pulse
sources.quote: If your pulse feels irregular, you should check for a full 60 seconds.

sources.title: British Heart Foundation, Your heart rate
sources.quote: You may be able to tell if you have a normal or irregular heart rate by checking your pulse

plans.title: Racing heart that comes and goes

steps.text: A crewmate feels your pulse at the wrist for 60 seconds while the cameras count it.
Note when it starts and stops, how often it happens and what you were doing.
Avoid things that can trigger it, such as stress, caffeine and alcohol. This can help if it is not caused by a health condition.
Add an existing ECG report if there is one.
Measure your pulse at the camera station again, sitting still.
Measure your pulse with the kit oximeter: hand warm, relaxed and below heart level, sitting still, until it shows one steady number.
If it keeps coming back or happens more often, tell the medical officer.
Chest pain or discomfort with the racing heart
Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
Feeling faint or fainting
It is still there and does not go away (how long: threshold to be set by clinical review)
Any heart attack symptom
The medical officer reviews. Anything more, as in the onboard procedure.

plans.title: Eye injury or something in the eye

steps.text: Cover the other eye. Read the same text on the screen with each eye and record any difference. Test card and distance: to be set by clinical review.
steps.cannot_replace_text: This kit cannot examine the eye surface.

steps.text: Take a still, close photo of the eye in good light, kept for the medical officer and the log. Do not touch the eye.
steps.cannot_replace_text: This kit cannot examine the eye surface.

steps.text: Do not rub the eye.
If an object is stuck in the eye, do not remove it. Cover the eye with a rigid shield that rests on the bone around the eye, not on the eye.
Chemical, dust or grit in the eye: hold the eye open and rinse with lots of clean water at once, for at least 20 minutes.
In weightlessness, water and dust float. Use the onboard eye wash set. Until it is ready, rinse with a drink bag and soak up the water with towels.
A crewmate repeats the sight check and the photo, and keeps both for the log.

replaces_ground_task.quote: Ground support will be necessary in the follow up for the best case and in both the evaluation and follow up for the worst case scenario.

steps.text: Pain or a gritty feeling that does not settle after rinsing: tell the medical officer. How long to wait: to be set by clinical review.
Something stuck in the eye, a chemical in the eye, or any change in sight: call the medical officer at once.

replaces_ground_task.quote: Later diagnosis of damage will require ground communications.

steps.text: Remove a loose particle and check the eye surface for scratches, as in the onboard procedure.
Eye medicines, as in the onboard procedure.

prepare.text: What to prepare for the trip: to be set by flight rules.

steps.text: Keep each blood pressure reading with its time, so it can be compared with your own baseline.
Any heart attack symptom: press Someone needs help now. Every minute matters.
Chest pain, heaviness or discomfort
Pain or discomfort in the arms, back, shoulders, neck, jaw or above the belly button
Shortness of breath at rest or with little activity
Sweating a lot for no reason, nausea or vomiting, light-headedness or sudden dizziness
A racing heart with chest pain, shortness of breath or feeling faint
Collapse or no response
The medical officer reviews. Anything more, as in the onboard procedure.
Protect the next sleep period.
Rate your mood at each daily check, to see whether it persists.
If symptoms persist or do not go away, talk to the medical officer.
Chest pain
Shortness of breath
Feeling faint
Thoughts of death or suicide
The medical officer reviews. Anything more, as in the onboard procedure.

items.text: Ask for a private conversation with the ground, when the link allows.

steps.text: Keep the sleep space cool, dark and quiet.
No caffeine in the 6 to 12 hours before sleep, depending on the person.
In the 2 hours before sleep, avoid vigorous exercise and large or spicy meals, and avoid bright or blue-enriched light.
Wear the band overnight, and confirm or correct its estimate in the morning.
Thoughts of death or suicide
Nodding off during a task: tell a crewmate and stop any critical task now. The formal route is to be set by clinical and operations review.
Waking gasping or out of breath: tell the medical officer. Whether it should open Someone needs help is to be set by clinical review.
The medical officer reviews. Anything more, as in the onboard procedure.
Protect the next sleep period.
If you feel fatigued, keep up light exposure through the day.
Take the reaction test and compare it with your own usual. How much slower matters: threshold to be set by clinical review.
Thoughts of death or suicide
Nodding off during a task: tell a crewmate and stop any critical task now. The formal route is to be set by clinical and operations review.
The medical officer reviews. Anything more, as in the onboard procedure.
Report symptoms with their time.
If the cabin average stays above the limit over several days, follow the vehicle's procedure to find and repair degraded CO2 scrubbing or add supplemental scrubbing.

replaces_ground_task.quote: If the average ppCO2 is exceeded over several days for unknown reasons, the Flight Control Team will take corrective actions to either identify, diagnose, and repair degraded CO2 scrubbing equipment or activate supplemental CO2 scrubbing equipment as needed.

steps.text: Keep air moving around the face during sleep.
Headache with vision or eye problems, worse with coughing, sneezing, bending down or exercise, or with vomiting: tell the medical officer promptly.
A seizure
Numbness or weakness in the body or face
It started suddenly and is extremely painful
A head injury within the last 3 months
Difficulty speaking, balancing, walking or remembering
Drowsy or confused
Loss of vision
A very high temperature, a stiff neck, or bright light bothering the eyes
The medical officer reviews. Anything more, as in the onboard procedure.
In-flight eye checks are scheduled, and more can be done when clinically indicated. A new change in vision is a reason to ask for one.
Blurred or double vision, flashing lights or shapes, a dark shadow moving across the vision, pain in one or both eyes, or a headache with vision or eye problems: tell the medical officer promptly.
Suddenly cannot see from one or both eyes
Sudden severe eye pain
Headache with loss of vision
The medical officer decides on glasses of higher power, as in the onboard procedure.
